summary: Describes the architecture for protocols and services supporting Unmanned Aircraft System Remote ID and tracking, and related communications, meeting the requirements of RFC 9153.

plainLanguage.summary: A drone has to be able to announce who it is to anyone nearby, over a short radio link with very little room for data. This RFC describes how DRIP does that: the identifier is derived from the drone's own key, registered in the DNS like a domain name, and signed with a signature that is too long to copy from an earlier broadcast.

questions: how does drone remote id work
subtitle: How drones announce a verifiable identity in flight, using cryptographic identifiers, DNS registries and existing Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Regulators require unmanned aircraft to be remotely identifiable, but the broadcast links used for that are tiny, so a trustworthy, hard-to-spoof identifier is difficult to fit in.
tldr.mechanism: DRIP uses Hierarchical Host Identity Tags as self-asserting IPv6-style identifiers, registers them in DNS-based public and private registries, and signs broadcast messages so an Observer can build a chain of trust.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an architecture and entry point for the DRIP documents. It meets the requirements of RFC 9153 except the QoS requirement, which is left for future work.

today: RFC 9434 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023 with no obsoleting or updating documents. It frames the DRIP work and relies on RFC 9153 for the requirements and RFC 9374 for the entity tag.

sections.title: What Remote ID Has to Achieve
sections.content:
This document describes an architecture for protocols and services to support Unmanned Aircraft System Remote Identification and tracking, plus UAS-RID-related communications, taking into account current and proposed regulations and non-IETF technical standards. It adheres to the requirements listed in the DRIP Requirements document and illustrates how all of them can be met, except for GEN-7 QoS, which is left for future work. It also frames the DRIP Entity Tag within the architecture.

UAS RID is an application that enables unmanned aircraft to be identified by UAS Traffic Management, UAS Service Suppliers and third-party entities such as law enforcement. Many considerations, including safety and security, dictate that unmanned aircraft be remotely identifiable. Civil Aviation Authorities worldwide are mandating UAS RID, and they currently promulgate performance-based regulations that do not specify techniques but cite industry consensus technical standards as acceptable means of compliance.

The regulatory landscape is described in the document. The US Federal Aviation Administration published a Notice of Proposed Rule Making in 2019 and a Final Rule in 2021, imposing requirements on manufacturers and operators, commercial and recreational; the rule states that ADS-B Out and transponders cannot satisfy the UAS RID requirements on the aircraft it applies to. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency, pursuing the U-space concept of a single European airspace safely shared by manned and unmanned aircraft, published a delegated regulation in 2019 with UAS RID requirements and an implementing regulation with detailed rules, updated in 2021. ASTM International Technical Committee F38 developed the ASTM standard that defines one set of UAS RID information and two means of communicating it, MAC layer broadcast and IP layer network; if a unmanned aircraft uses both, the same information must be provided by both, and the FAA has accepted the corresponding Means of Compliance with some caveats. The 3rd Generation Partnership Project completed its UAS RID requirement study in Release 16 and followed with enhanced requirements and architecture support for 4G and 5G networks in Release 17, with further enhancements in Release 18.

DRIP is meant to leverage existing Internet resources, standard protocols, services, infrastructures and business models, and to specify how to apply IETF standards to complement the external standards. The document closes the gaps between the regulators' concepts of operations and the external standard as they relate to Internet technologies and direct radio communications. The issues it lists are the design of trustworthy remote identifiers, especially for use as single-use session IDs; mechanisms to use the DNS for registering and publishing public and private information; specific authentication methods and message payload formats that let a receiver verify that a Broadcast RID message came from the claimed sender and that the sender is in the claimed registry; harvesting Broadcast RID messages for inclusion in traffic management, with the optional Crowdsourced Remote ID extension; methods for instantly establishing secure communications between an Observer and the pilot of an observed unmanned aircraft; and privacy in the messages. The document should serve as a main point of entry into the set of IETF documents addressing the basic DRIP requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Aviation regulators in several jurisdictions now require that a drone broadcast an identity that anyone nearby can check, and that the same identity be available over the Internet to services that track the airspace. The rules do not say how to build it; they point at industry standards. DRIP is the IETF's answer to filling in the parts those standards leave to the Internet.

sections.title: Two Ways to Report a Drone
sections.content:
The specification introduces two types of UAS Remote ID, as defined in the ASTM standard.

Broadcast RID is a set of messages for direct, one-way broadcast transmissions from the unmanned aircraft over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, currently defined as MAC layer messages. Internet or other wide area network connectivity is only needed for registry information lookup by Observers using the directly received identifier. Broadcast RID should be functionally usable in situations with no Internet connectivity. It provides information only about aircraft within direct radio frequency line of sight, typically similar to visual line of sight, with a range up to approximately 1 km. The information may be harvested from received broadcasts and made available over the Internet, which enables surveillance of areas too large for local direct observation.

Network RID uses the same data dictionary as the basis of Broadcast RID messages. The information to be reported is generated by the unmanned aircraft, typically some of it by the aircraft and some by the ground control station, for example their respective locations derived from GNSS. The information is sent by the aircraft or the ground control station to the cognizant Network Remote Identification Service Provider, typically the service supplier under which the unmanned aircraft is operating if it is participating in traffic management. That provider publishes, via the Discovery and Synchronization Service over the Internet, that it has operations in various four-dimensional airspace volumes, describing the volumes but not the operations. An Observer's device, expected but not specified to be based on the Web, queries a Network Remote Identification Display Provider, typically also a service supplier, about any operations in a specific four-dimensional airspace volume. Using fully specified Web-based methods, the display provider queries all service providers with operations in intersecting volumes, aggregates what they return, and responds to the Observer's query.

Command and control must flow from the ground control station to the aircraft, typically over a direct radio link today, though with increasing beyond visual line of sight operations it is expected often to be a wireless link at each end with the Internet between. Telemetry, at least position and heading, flows back along the reverse path, so RID information for both the aircraft and the ground control station can be sent by whichever has Internet connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways a drone's identity reaches you. Broadcast RID is the drone shouting to anyone in radio range, about a kilometre. Network RID is the same information travelling over the Internet through the flight service operator, so that anyone can query a map area and learn what is flying there.

sections.title: The Hierarchical Host Identity Tag
sections.content:
The architecture uses Hierarchical Host Identity Tags as self-asserting IPv6 addresses suitable as a UAS identifier type and, more generally, as trustworthy multipurpose remote identifiers. Self-asserting here means that, given the Host Identity, the HHIT construction and a signature by the registry on the HHIT and Host Identity, the HHIT can be verified by the receiver as a trusted identifier. The explicit registration hierarchy within the HHIT provides registration discovery to yield the Host Identity for third-party validation or to prove that the HHIT and Host Identity have been registered uniquely.

The problem is a tight space. Broadcast RID, especially its support for Bluetooth 4, imposes severe constraints. A previous revision of the ASTM standard allowed identifiers of types 1, 2 and 3, each of 20 bytes. The current standard adds type 4, Specific Session ID, for other standards bodies to extend it; type 4 uses one byte to index the subtype, leaving 19 bytes, and ASTM has allocated Specific Session ID subtype 1 to IETF DRIP. The maximum ASTM UAS RID Authentication Message payload is 201 bytes each for Authentication Types 1, 2, 3 and 4, and Type 5 is added for other standards bodies with a Specific Authentication Method; with Type 5, one of the 201 bytes indexes the method type, leaving only 200 bytes for DRIP authentication payloads, including one or more identifiers and associated authentication data.

Only two kinds of IP-address-compatible identifier are cryptographically derived from the public keys of the entities they identify: Cryptographically Generated Addresses and Host Identity Tags, and neither has registration and retrieval capability. Each HHIT therefore embeds plaintext information designating the hierarchy within which it is registered, and a cryptographic hash of that information concatenated with the entity's public key. Hash collisions may occur, but the registry can detect them and reject registration requests rather than issue credentials, for example by enforcing a First Come First Served policy. Preimage attacks are mitigated by the registration process, which locks the HHIT to a specific Host Identity.

The proof of ownership comes from an asymmetric key pair: the identifier is derived directly from the public key, and ownership is guaranteed by signing that identifier with the associated private key. The association between identifier and key is ensured by binding the public key to the identifier, since the identifier results from the hash of the public key. The public key is the Host Identity and the identifier is the Host Identity Tag. By construction the tag is statistically unique through the mandatory use of hash functions with second-preimage resistance, and the cryptographically bound addition of the hierarchy and the registration process give complete global uniqueness: registration forces an attacker to generate the same public key rather than a different key that produces the same tag.

An aircraft equipped for Broadcast RID MUST be provisioned with its HHIT, the Host Identity public key it was derived from, and the corresponding private key for signing. The private key resides only in the ultimate source of Network RID messages: if the ground control station is the source, the station MUST hold the key, and if the aircraft is the source and the station relays, the aircraft MUST hold it. A self-endorsement of an HHIT used as an identifier can be done in as little as 88 bytes when Ed25519 is used, by including only the 16-byte HHIT, two 4-byte timestamps and the 64-byte signature. Ed25519 is the mandatory-to-implement signing algorithm, because the requirements can best be met by restricting the Host Identity to 32 bytes; a larger public key would rule out the offline endorsement feature that fits within the 200-byte maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier is a hash of the drone's own public key, so it proves who sent it to anyone who can check a signature. Two things make it work in practice: the hash encodes which registry issued it, and the registry refuses to issue the same identifier twice. With Ed25519, an aircraft can sign its own identity in 88 bytes, which fits in the tiny broadcast message the rules allow.

sections.title: Registration and the Two Registries
sections.content:
DRIP registries hold both public and private unmanned aircraft information resulting from the registration process. Because the uses differ, and to improve scalability, security and simplicity of administration, the public and private information can be stored in different registries. The entity that performs the registry role is called a DRIP Identity Management Entity, which vets claims and evidence from a registrant and delivers endorsements and certificates in response. It is a high-level entity that can hold the role of HHIT Domain Authority, Registered Assigning Authority, or root of trust, typically the HHIT prefix owner or DNS apex owner.

The public information registry provides trustworthy information such as endorsements of ownership and registration with the domain authority. Optionally, pointers to the registries implicit in the identifier can be included. This public information is principally used by Observers of Broadcast RID messages; data on aircraft that only use Network RID is available through the network display provider, which is the only source of information for a query on an airspace volume. A DRIP identifier MUST be registered as an Internet domain name, at an arbitrary level in the hierarchy, so that the DNS can provide all the needed public information. A standardized HHIT fully qualified domain name can deliver the Host Identity via a HIP resource record, and other public information such as the authority and assignment PTR records and HIP rendezvous servers. These public registries can use DNSSEC to deliver public information that is not inherently trustworthy. The DNS entry can also provide a revocation service, for example by returning a record showing that the identity has been revoked instead of the Host Identity record.

The private information registry holds information similar to that required for Internet domain name registration. It is expected to be provided by the same organizations that run a service supplier, likely integrated with it, and the lookup function may be implemented by the network display providers. When a DRIP Entity Tag is used as an aircraft's Session ID, the corresponding manufacturer-assigned serial number MUST be stored in a private registry that can be identified uniquely from the tag; when the tag is used as either a Session ID or a serial number and the operation is flown under traffic management, the corresponding operational intent identifier SHOULD be stored there as well. Other information MAY be stored, and often must be, to satisfy regulator requirements or operator policies.

The private registry supports the essential operations of add, delete, update and query using interoperable open standard protocols, by leveraging aspects of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol and the Registry Data Access Protocol. The registry in which a given unmanned aircraft is registered needs to be findable starting from the identifier, using the methods specified in RFC 9224. Alternative methods are possible: an access-controlled DNS, for example over DNS over TLS, and WebFinger, which may be used by a display provider with specific customers.
sections.plainLanguage: The drone's identifier is registered like a domain name, so the DNS can answer questions about it. Some answers are public, such as who vouched for the drone, and are protected with DNSSEC where they are not signed by the issuer. Others are private, such as the serial number or the flight's permit, and are held in a registry that the operator controls and that is found through standard registration protocols.

sections.title: Building Trust, and the Security Considerations
sections.content:
While the entity identifier is self-asserting, it alone does not provide the trustworthiness that UAS RID needs: non-repudiation, protection against spoofing, message integrity, scalability. For that it MUST be registered and actively used by the party. A sender's identity cannot be proved merely by its possessing a tag and broadcasting it as a claim, and sending data signed with that key's private key proves little, since it is subject to trivial replay attacks using previously broadcast messages. Only sending the tag together with a signature over novel data, data that changes frequently and cannot be predicted, and that the Observer can validate externally, such as a signed location and vector message matching what the Observer actually sees, proves that the observed aircraft holds the private key and therefore the claimed identifier.

From the received messages and information looked up using the received identifier in online registries or local caches, it is possible to establish levels of trust in the asserted information and the operator. A combination of different DRIP Authentication Messages lets an Observer validate the identifier in real time, online or offline. Some messages contain the relevant registration of the identifier in the claimed registry; some contain sender signatures over both static data such as registration and dynamically changing data such as current location. Combining the two lets the Observer piece together a chain of trust, including real-time evidence to judge the claims.

The security considerations add several warnings. The size of the public key hash in the HHIT is vulnerable to a second-preimage attack: it is well within current server array technology to compute another key pair that hashes to the same tag, given the current construction length. So a receiver that only checks that the received Host Identity hashes to the received tag could be fooled; online receivers should instead verify the pair with the domain authority it claims registration with, and both online and offline receivers can use a chain of endorsements from a root of trust through the authority and the domain authority to the aircraft. Compromise of a registry's private key could do widespread harm by letting bad actors impersonate trusted members of that registry. All DRIP public keys can be found in the DNS and therefore revoked there, and users SHOULD check the DNS when available, though specific revocation procedures are yet to be determined.

On private key physical security, the security provided by asymmetric techniques depends on protecting the private keys. The ground control station may need the key pair to register the identifier, so it may be the station that generates the key and hands it to the aircraft, which makes the station part of the key security boundary. Leakage of the private key to the component manufacturer is a valid concern. Since a small harmless aircraft could be carried by a larger dangerous one as a false flag, secure storage of the private key is out of scope here.

On quantum resistance, there has been no effort in DRIP so far to address post-quantum cryptography, because small unmanned aircraft and Broadcast RID are so constrained that current post-quantum cryptography is not applicable. Since an aircraft may use a unique identifier for each operation, the attack window can be limited to the duration of the operation. One potential future use is key pairs with long usage lives that rarely need to be transmitted over constrained links, and because the identifier contains the ID of the cryptographic suite used in its creation, a future algorithm that fits the constraints may be readily added.

On denial of service, remote ID services from the aircraft use a wireless link in a public space and are open to radio jamming; it is trivial for an attacker to stop any aircraft messages from reaching a receiver, so it is pointless to try to provide relief from denial-of-service attacks, since there is always the ultimate jamming attack. On spoofing and replay, spoofing is combatted by the self-attesting properties of the identifiers plus registration, and a receiver MUST NOT trust any claims received from an observed aircraft, not even the basic identifier message, until it has verified that the private key used to sign the claims is trusted, that the sender actually holds that key, and that the sender appears to be the observed aircraft. That requires a complete chain of endorsements from a root of trust to the leaf tag, plus a message containing suitable nonce-like data signed with the private key. Nonce-like data is readily available to the prover and verifier, changes frequently, is not predictable by the prover, and can be checked quickly at low cost.
sections.plainLanguage: Having a cryptographically derived identifier is not enough on its own, because anyone can replay an old broadcast. The proof has to be tied to something new and checkable, such as a signed position and heading that matches what the receiver can actually observe. The RFC also spells out the limits: the hash is short enough that a second preimage could be computed, so a receiver that is online should ask the registry, and the registry's own keys are worth protecting.

sections.title: Harvesting Broadcasts and Contacting the Pilot
sections.content:
The document describes how to bring broadcast messages into traffic management, and how to reach the people behind an observed aircraft.

Regulators are expected to require both Broadcast RID and Network RID for large unmanned aircraft, while allowing the operator's choice for small ones; the FAA permits only Broadcast RID for rule compliance but encourages Network RID for complementary functionality, especially in support of traffic management. One opportunity is to enhance the architecture with gateways from Broadcast RID to Network RID, which gives regulators and operators flexibility and offers greater fidelity than Network RID reporting of planned area operations, together with surveillance of areas too large for local direct observation. These gateways could be pre-positioned around airports, public gatherings and other sensitive areas, or crowdsourced, since nothing more than a smartphone with a suitable application is needed. Crowdsourcing can be encouraged by a quid pro quo that provides the outputs of the surveillance data service only to the finders that contributed.

Two entities are defined for this. A CS-RID Finder is the gateway for Broadcast Remote ID messages into traffic management, performing this function via a CS-RID Surveillance Supplemental Data Service Provider; it could implement, integrate or accept outputs from a Broadcast RID receiver, and should not depend on a direct interface with a ground control station, service provider, display provider or client. The CS-RID SDSP aggregates and processes information collected by Finders, for example estimating aircraft locations by multilateration, and presents the same interfaces to service and display providers as they present to each other, but its data source must be readily distinguishable as coming through Finders rather than directly from the aircraft.

Because the broadcast media have a limited range, messages claiming sender locations far from the physical receiver should arouse suspicion of an intent to deceive, and a fast, cheap consistency check can compare the claimed location against the receiver's own location, with authorities alerted to failed checks. The SDSP can use messages with precise date, time and position stamps from the gateways to multilaterate aircraft locations, independently of the locations claimed in the messages, which are self-reported by the operator and subject to time lag, error, misconfiguration or deliberate deception. Multilateration uses physical layer information such as the precise time of arrival of transmissions at receivers whose locations are known in advance. Gateways with additional sensors, such as smartphones with cameras, can provide independent information on the aircraft type and size, confirming or refuting claims made in the messages.

For contact, a DRIP identifier based on an HHIT embeds an identifier of the registry in which it can be found, expected typically to be the service supplier under which the aircraft is flying, and the procedures of the trust section let an Observer verify that relationship. With suitable records in the public and private registries, a lookup can return not only information about the aircraft but also the identities of and pointers to the associated entities, including locators, typically IP addresses, by which they can be reached. A suitably equipped Observer could then open a secure channel, for example over IPsec or HIP, and use any standard higher-layer protocol, such as SIP, for Observer to Pilot communications. Two preconditions are needed: each party needs a currently usable way, typically the DNS, to resolve the other's identifier to a currently usable locator, and there must be currently usable bidirectional IP connectivity between them.
sections.plainLanguage: Two services build on the broadcast. The first collects what nearby phones hear and turns it into an Internet feed, so a city or a national forest can be watched rather than one street at a time; the receiving phone's own location is a check on what the drone claims about itself. The second lets an observer who spots a drone open a secure line to the pilot, using the same identifier system to find out who is operating it.

viz.caption: THE SECURITY AND PRIVACY POINTS THE RFC MAKES

items.title: Second-preimage attack
items.text: The hash in the identifier is short enough that another key pair could be computed with the same value, so online receivers should check the pair with the registry.

items.title: Registry key compromise
items.text: A stolen registry private key lets an attacker impersonate trusted members of that registry; the public keys live in the DNS and can be revoked there.

items.title: Private key custody
items.text: The ground control station may have to generate the key and hand it to the aircraft, which puts it inside the key security boundary.

items.title: Quantum resistance
items.text: Not addressed yet; current post-quantum cryptography does not fit the size limits, but a fresh identifier per operation limits the attack window.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: Radio jamming always wins, so the document does not promise relief from denial-of-service attacks.

items.title: Replay protection
items.text: Claims are trusted only after a chain of endorsements and a signature over data that changes and cannot be predicted.
